titre_video: Top 10 Insane Dark Web Conspiracies That Were Actually True All Along

segments.titre: The Dark Web as a trap built by the state
segments.resume: Intro: the Dark Web is supposed to be a lawless frontier beyond the reach of authorities, but the video claims the state built it and owns the map. For years the world's most dangerous criminals trading billions in stolen data and crypto thought they were untouchable while walking blindly into a trap.
segments.texte: The Dark Web is supposed to be a lawless frontier. An invisible space the authorities can’t touch you. The truth is infinitely worse. The state built it, they own the map, and they’re just waiting for you to cross the border. For years, the world's most dangerous criminals thought they were untouchable, trading billions in stolen data and crypto. But they weren’t hiding. They were walking blindly into a trap.

segments.titre: 10. Hitman marketplaces: Besa Mafia and 'Etsy for hitmen'
segments.resume: Dark sites such as Besa Mafia and Camorra Hitman advertise themselves as the number one hitman marketplace, offering bespoke packages including torture. The Times reported that one site took over half a million dollars from customers who paid for the assassinations of 175 people, though most such sites are now defunct and the vast majority are scams.
segments.texte: 10. Dark websites such as Besa Mafia, Camorra Hitman, often advertising themselves as the #1 Hitman Marketplace. They’ve even been called an “Etsy for hitmen.” They can look surprisingly legitimate, offering services like the traditional bullet to the head. But for the right amount of cash, a customer can order a bespoke package -- a variety of torture that precedes a variety of kinds of murder. The Times newspaper in the UK reported that just one of these websites had taken in over half a million dollars. Every cent came from customers who had collectively paid for the assassinations of 175 people. The people are genuine. The targets were real. The hitman service wasn’t… well not always. It’s thought most of these sites no longer function and everyone knows the vast majority are scams. But people are still ordering murders on the Dark Web.

segments.titre: Dutch journalists find real hitman orders in 2025
segments.resume: In 2025 Dutch journalists obtained hacked data from a Dark Web hitman site and found at least seven concrete orders to murder people in the Netherlands, with four customers already paid. Victims included a nurse, a teacher and a civil servant, at prices of $1,200 to $11,700, and the family of a nurse targeted by Imran M. had to hide for six months.
segments.texte: In 2025, Dutch journalists obtained hacked data from a Dark Web hitman site and discovered at least 7 concrete orders to murder people in the Netherlands. Four customers had already paid up. The intended victims weren't part of organized crime. One was a nurse. One was a teacher and another a civil servant. The price paid for their death was between $1,200 and $11,700. One of the customers wrote, “I want you to burn him alive,”. Another client told the assassin he didn’t care if someone else got hurt in the crossfire: “All I want is for him to die; I don’t care what happens to the mother.” But here’s the thing. The police couldn’t be sure if all these websites were fake. When a man named Imran M. ordered his ex-girlfriend nurse be killed, even offering with a $500 bonus if they could do it at the weekend , the woman and her family were forced into hiding for 6 months. You might have been told these sites are all phony and police don’t fear anyone will actually die, but it’s always not the case. The contract killing marketplace is alive and well and as a Dutch investigator told the press, they take “these matters very seriously.” And it’s a problem that seems to be everywhere.

segments.titre: 9. Kristy Felkins and the Besa Mafia hack
segments.resume: American Kristy Lynn Felkins sent 12 bitcoins to Besa Mafia to have her husband killed, expecting a life insurance payout. When hacker bRpsd leaked data of 250 user accounts, the FBI read almost 2,700 messages, found 38 supposed hits and a folder of victim photos, and concluded the site was fake.
segments.texte: 9. If you think the authorities are only hunting hitmen overseas, think again. Dark Web assassins are being hired in the U.S., by Americans who forget they have digital footprints. 38 year old Kristy Lynn Felkins sent Besa Mafia 12 bitcoins. If she’d waited and sold today, those coins would be worth over $929,000. But instead of waiting to become a millionaire, she gave her coins to a fake hitman to have her husband killed. She was willing to pay a $4,000 bonus if the assassin did it immediately. Make it look like a mugging, she wrote, and told them not to worry about harming her ex’s new lover. Money wasn’t an issue. Once he was dead, she’d come into a very handsome life insurance policy. Felkins was using a hidden service on the Tor network where the data is anonymized and users are supposed to be anonymous. But that doesn’t matter if the website is breached and you’ve supplied the name and location of your soon-to-be-assassinated husband. When a hacker calling himself “bRpsd” hacked Besa Mafia and leaked the data of 250 user accounts, the FBI soon intervened. The agents read almost 2,700 personal messages between admin and customers. Many were about the 38 hits that were supposedly in process. There was even a “victims” folder with photographs of all the marks. This time, the FBI knew that the website was a fake.

segments.titre: FBI honeypot theory and Felkins's sentence
segments.resume: Some people believe the FBI creates hitman sites as honeypots to prevent murders, which is unconfirmed, and entrapment laws could make it hard in court. Felkins got 5 years because she believed the Dark Web would protect her identity, and the video moves on to cases where hitmen were 100% real.
segments.texte: Some people believe the FBI itself creates these websites as honeypots so they can prevent murders but so far that’s unconfirmed. Laws around entrapment could make that difficult for them in court. But when hackers do the work for them: no problem. Kristy Felkins got 5 years because ultimately, she believed the Dark Web would protect her identity. As you’ll see throughout this video, that’s often not the case at all. But first, let’s break the current trend of claiming that all Dark Web hitmen are fake and tell you some stories about when they were 100% real.

segments.titre: 8. Jim Bell's Assassination Politics
segments.resume: The idea of anonymously funding murder began with American engineer and crypto-anarchist Jim Bell, whose mid-1990s essay Assassination Politics proposed crowdfunding the deaths of government officials with encrypted digital cash. He argued the world would be better without corrupt officials if one person in a thousand paid $1.
segments.texte: 8. That’s a lot of fake sites on the Dark Web but the idea of using the internet to anonymously fund murder was originally very real. It started with an American engineer and crypto-anarchist named Jim Bell. In the mid-1990s, he wrote an essay titled Assassination Politics. He proposed anonymously crowdfunding the deaths of government officials using encrypted digital cash, then in its infancy. No one would know who had contributed the money or who had carried out the killing. According to Bell, the world would be a better place without corrupt public officials. He wrote, “If only 0.1% of the population, or one person in a thousand, was willing to pay $1 to see some government slimeball dead.”

segments.titre: The Assassination Market and Kuwabatake Sanjuro
segments.resume: In 2013 Kuwabatake Sanjuro created the Assassination Market, where users added Bitcoin to bounties on targets and predicted the date of their death, with the obvious incentive to make the prediction come true. Reported targets included Ben Bernanke, Barack Obama and Keith Alexander, and Sanjuro eventually withdrew Bitcoin worth over a million dollars.
segments.texte: He was serious. But it wasn’t until 2013, when the Dark Web was in full flow, that someone calling themselves Kuwabatake Sanjuro created the Assassination Market. Based on Bell’s idea, it included a system where users predicted when someone would die. People contributed Bitcoin to a bounty on a target and could secretly post the exact date that person would die. If they were correct, they collected the bounty. There was, of course, one obvious way of making sure your prediction came true… Kill the person yourself. These weren’t imaginary targets, either. Bounties were reportedly placed on people including Federal Reserve chairman Ben Bernanke, President Barack Obama and NSA director Keith Alexander. Sanjuro was quite open about what he wanted to achieve, writing: “I will be satisfied when all governments, all politicians, and all armies are destroyed.” People made plenty of predictions but he gave up and took all the Bitcoin out once it was worth well over a million dollars. This gave birth to the assassin-for-hire phenomenon that together exposed that a lot of regular people were willing to pay to have someone killed. But if you really wanted someone dead, you didn’t go to hitman websites.

segments.titre: Russian teens hired to kill investigator Yevgeniya Shishkina
segments.resume: In 2018 two Russian men aged 17 and 19 were arrested for killing Yevgeniya Shishkina, a top investigator probing a Dark Web drug trafficking operation, shot on her Moscow doorstep. One teen posted a resume on a Dark Web site and was offered $15,000 in crypto, and one had to watch a YouTube video to load the gun from a dead-drop.
segments.texte: You trawled Dark Web forums looking for wayward teens. In 2018, two Russian men, aged 17 and 19, were arrested after assassinating a top Russian investigator who was looking into a Dark Web drug trafficking operation. The men had been hired after talking with a gang boss. They were paid in bitcoin and the victim, Yevgeniya Shishkina, was gunned down on her doorstep outside her Moscow apartment. One of the teens had posted his resume on a Dark Web site and that was how he ended up being offered $15,000 in crypto for the hit. Both boys were not exactly skilled operators. One even had to watch a YouTube video to see how to load the modified gun that he’d picked up at a dead-drop. So, Dark Web hitmen are real… if you know where to look for them.

segments.titre: Finland's first online-arranged contract killing
segments.resume: In 2021 Finn Markus Aleksi Hytönen offered his services as a killer on the Dark Web and was hired by 20-year-old Atu Viljami Halonen to kill Halonen's father for about $11,000. Hytönen stabbed the father more than 40 times on CCTV, and both received life sentences, in what Yle called the first proven online-arranged contract killing in Finland.
segments.texte: In 2021, 19-year-old Finn, Markus Aleksi Hytönen, didn’t post his resume to a Dark Web forum but offered his services as a killer. He was contacted by 20-year-old Atu Viljami Halonen who promised him the equivalent of about $11,000 to murder his father. Hytönen went through with it. He stabbed and slashed the father more than 40 times, all of which was watched by CCTV cameras. Police soon found out the 2 young men had met each other online and arranged the contract killing through the Tor network. Both were eventually sentenced to life in prison: Hytönen for murder and Halonen for soliciting it. According to Finnish broadcaster Yle, it was the first proven contract killing in Finland to have been arranged online. So, Dark Web hitmen are not an urban legend.

segments.titre: Italian acid plot and Europol's violence-as-a-service warning
segments.resume: In 2021 Italian police arrested a man who paid €10,000 in Bitcoin to a Dark Web assassin to pour acid on his ex-girlfriend, and Europol's crypto-analysis identified the Bitcoin buyer. Europol warned that organized criminals use young, inexperienced men for violence, recruited on the Dark Web, social media and encrypted apps, a trend called violence-as-a-service.
segments.texte: And here’s something even more disturbing. In 2021, Italian police arrested a man who had hired a Dark Web assassin to pour acid over his ex-girlfriend and leave her paralyzed. The price? €10,000 in Bitcoin. Police intercepted the plot before she was harmed. Meanwhile, Europol performed what it called an “urgent, complex crypto-analysis” that helped identify who had bought the Bitcoin. They said that across Europe, organized criminals have been turning to young, inexperienced men to carry out violence. They warned in 2021 that the use of younger and inexperienced hitmen was becoming a serious issue. Sometimes they’re recruited on the Dark Web. Sometimes through social media and encrypted messaging apps, in what authorities have called violence-as-a-service.

segments.titre: Why teen hitmen get caught: amateur mistakes
segments.resume: Young people are offered tens of thousands to commit shootings and murders for criminals they never met. The Russian and Finnish killers were not caught by cracking Tor but through ordinary forensic mistakes like CCTV, and criminology professor David Wilson says economically desperate young men take these jobs.
segments.texte: Young people can be offered money -- sometimes tens of thousands -- to carry out shootings and murders for criminals they’ve never even met. The 2 Russian killers and the teenagers in Finland weren’t caught because someone had cracked Tor. They were caught because they were amateurs who made ordinary forensic mistakes and failed to account for things like CCTV. And there are plenty more kids just like them. As criminology professor David Wilson told Harper’s in 2020, a surprising number of “economically desperate young men are willing to take on these brutal jobs.” But compared to what you’re about to hear, these teenage assassins are small-time players in the larger world of Dark Web crime.

segments.titre: 7. Alexandre Cazes: the AlphaBay creator's lavish life
segments.resume: In the 2010s Canadian Alexandre Cazes lived in Thailand with a Lamborghini Aventador, a Porsche, properties in several countries and millions in crypto, with a net worth of $23 million by 25. A college dropout from Trois-Rivières who started the IT business EBX Technologies, he built AlphaBay from Thailand.
segments.texte: 7. In the 2010s, Alexandre “Alex” Cazes, a 20-something-year-old Canadian, was living his “best life.” He could be seen tearing around Thailand in a Lamborghini Aventador, sometimes at terrifying speeds, while living with his Thai wife in a luxury home. He owned a Porsche, properties in several countries, and millions of dollars in cryptocurrency. By the age of 25, his own financial records put his net worth at $23 million. Not bad for a college dropout. As a teenager growing up with his mother in Trois-Rivières, Canada, Cazes had skipped a grade and was sometimes described as a “little genius.” He studied computing at college but left to start his own IT business, EBX Technologies, building websites, hosting servers and repairing computers. Then, at around 18 or 19, he moved to Thailand, leaving what he called a “broken society” for something more traditional. And it was from Thailand that the computer genius would build one of the biggest criminal marketplaces on Earth: AlphaBay.

segments.titre: AlphaBay: Amazon for the Dark Web
segments.resume: AlphaBay launched in 2014 and reached 14,000 users in 90 days, then hundreds of thousands of users and over 250,000 drug and chemical listings by 2017. It had over 100,000 listings for stolen identities, hacking tools, firearms and more, handled $600,000 to $800,000 daily and became bigger than Silk Road, with Cazes taking commissions.
segments.texte: Launched in 2014 when Cazes was just 23, AlphaBay was essentially Amazon for the Dark Web. Within 90 days, it reportedly had 14,000 users. By 2017, it had hundreds of thousands of users and more than 250,000 listings for illegal drugs and toxic chemicals alone. You name it, AlphaBay sold it. There were more than 100,000 listings for stolen identities, counterfeit goods, hacking tools, fraudulent documents, firearms and many, many other illegal products. An estimated $600,000 to $800,000 worth of transactions were taking place every single day. AlphaBay had become even bigger than the Dark Web OG, Silk Road. Cazes took commissions for the sales. That’s how he ended up driving a Lamborghini.

segments.titre: Cazes's fatal mistake: pimp_alex_91@hotmail.com
segments.resume: AlphaBay's welcome and password-reset emails exposed in their headers the address pimp_alex_91@hotmail.com, which investigators linked to Alexandre Cazes. A 2008 post on a French-language forum showed his real name with the same address and the username Alpha02, which he later used as AlphaBay administrator.
segments.texte: But while AlphaBay prided itself on security, its creator had made an almost comically stupid mistake. The genius, it transpired, was also a part-time idiot. When AlphaBay first started sending welcome and password-reset emails, information hidden in the email headers exposed an address belonging to its administrator: pimp_alex_91@hotmail.com Not exactly the kind of anonymous email address you'd expect from the man operating the world's nastiest marketplace. Investigators soon discovered that Pimp_Alex_91 was associated with a Canadian computer programmer named Alexandre Cazes. They then dug into the ancient internet and found posts Cazes had made on a French-language computer forum back in 2008, when he was still a teenager. At the bottom of one he'd helpfully left his real name: Alexandre Cazes: pimp_alex_91@hotmail.com And the username he'd been posting under: Alpha02. Years later, the creator and administrator of AlphaBay was using the name...you guessed it: Alpha02. He had effectively left investigators a trail of breadcrumbs that led right to the doorstep of his flash Bangkok home. Now they just needed to catch him… preferably with his computer open.

segments.titre: The 2017 arrest in Bangkok
segments.resume: In 2017 Thai police, with the FBI and DEA, prepared to arrest Cazes while Canadian authorities targeted AlphaBay's infrastructure. They first caused an outage so Cazes had to open his computer, and on July 5th they raided his house to find his unencrypted laptop open and him logged in as admin.
segments.texte: By 2017, investigators had secured warrants and an international operation was underway. Canadian authorities were targeting AlphaBay's infrastructure while Thai police, assisted by the FBI and DEA, prepared to arrest Cazes at his Bangkok mansion. The cops were smart, though. They didn’t just jump in. First, they created a service outage for AlphaBay which meant Cazes had to access his computer and bring his empire back online. The alternatives could have been him shutting everything down. On July 5th, Thai officers descended on his house. Sure enough, his laptop was open and he hadn’t encrypted the information on it. He was actually logged into AlphaBay as Admin. They caught him in the middle of trying to reboot the system and even responding to messages from annoyed users. His empire had come crashing down.

segments.titre: Cazes's net worth file and death in jail
segments.resume: Cazes kept a file listing his net worth of over £23 million, his cryptocurrencies, cash and more than $12.5 million in vehicles and real estate, telling police what to seize. The US wanted him extradited on racketeering, narcotics, identity theft, fraud and money laundering charges, but he was found dead in his jail cell a week after arrest.
segments.texte: Inside the computer, investigators found everything they needed. And if that wasn't enough, Cazes had helpfully created what amounted to an inventory of his criminal fortune. At the top it listed his total net worth, over £23 million. It also had his cryptocurrencies, cash and more than $12.5 million worth of vehicles and real estate. The police knew exactly what to seize. He was finished. At 25 years old, the US now wanted him extradited on charges including racketeering, narcotics distribution, identity theft, fraud and money laundering. He never made it to the U.S. Just a week after his arrest, Cazes was found dead in his jail cell. AlphaBay was dead.

segments.titre: AlphaBay returns: DeSnake and AlphaBay 2.0
segments.resume: Four years later people received the message that AlphaBay was back, run by a figure calling himself DeSnake who claimed to be the original number-two administrator and offered cryptographic evidence. AlphaBay 2.0 had new security mechanisms to survive server seizures and banned fentanyl, porn, COVID vaccines and hitmen.
segments.texte: Or so everyone thought... Because 4 years later, people began receiving the message: AlphaBay is back in action! A mysterious figure calling himself DeSnake was now the boss. He claimed he’d once been the original number-two administrator and security specialist. Then the new DeSnake dropped a bombshell. He was able to provide cryptographic evidence linking them to the old AlphaBay. If it was an impostor, it was a convincing one. A smart one, too. AlphaBay 2.0 incorporated new security mechanisms intended to allow the market to survive even if its servers were seized. And so as not to pique the interest of police too much, this version was almost ethical: no fentanyl, no porn, no COVID vaccines, no hitmen. It seemed that even the Dark Web had standards. Or… DeSnake wasn’t who he said he was.

segments.titre: Was DeSnake a law-enforcement honeypot?
segments.resume: The new owner may have avoided dangerous items because DeSnake could be law enforcement. In February 2023 AlphaBay went offline and DeSnake vanished, leaving the theory that police let criminals come to them instead of tracking them across the Dark Web.
segments.texte: Maybe the new owner didn’t want to sell very dangerous items because…well… DeSnake might be law enforcement. In February 2023, AlphaBay suddenly went offline. DeSnake vanished and has never been heard from since. Was he really the former AlphaBay administrator he claimed to be? Or was he a law-enforcement honeypot catching criminals doing business on his marketplace? Instead of spending years trying to identify criminals scattered across the Dark Web, maybe the criminals came to them. It’s a theory, and as you’ll see now, there’s a reason why many people believe it’s true.

segments.titre: 6. Dutch police take over Hansa: Operation Bayonet
segments.resume: After AlphaBay fell in 2017, buyers and sellers migrated to Hansa, which Dutch police had secretly taken over, impersonating the old administrators and running an efficient help desk. Gert Ras of the Dutch National High Tech Crime Unit said service quality went up, and after 27 days and about 27,000 transactions police shut it down as part of Operation Bayonet.
segments.texte: 6. When the original AlphaBay went down in 2017 that left a lot of people scrambling to get their fixes. But there was a solution. Most sellers and buyers migrated to another Dark Web marketplace called Hansa. But Hansa had one very serious flaw. The Dutch police had secretly taken control of it. And they had studied the old administrators' communications carefully enough to impersonate them perfectly. From being run by 2 old school cyber-criminals now a group of hardworking officers were in charge. For customers, Hansa had never run so seamlessly. One of the officers used work as an IT help-desk support. Now he’d taken over that part of Hansa he very efficiently dealt with their complaints and resolved disputes between dealers and customers. According to Gert Ras, head of the Dutch National High Tech Crime Unit: “The quality really went up… Everyone was very satisfied with the level of service they got.” For weeks, thousands of criminals fleeing their favorite marketplace were voluntarily opening accounts on Hansa. After 27 days and approximately 27,000 transactions, they shut it down… but for those 27 days, the investigators were having a blast. Operation Bayonet, which encompassed all the operations we’ve talked about, had given police the keys to the kingdom. They’d beaten the Dark Web at its own game. So, was AlphaBay 2.0 police in disguise? We don’t know, but it was very possible. Now let’s turn to one of the darkest aspects of this already dark corner of reality…

segments.titre: 5. Rhysida ransomware attack on Lurie Children's Hospital
segments.resume: In January 2024 the Rhysida ransomware group attacked Lurie Children's Hospital in Chicago, taking down phones, email, medical records and the patient portal and delaying surgeries. Rhysida claimed to have stolen around 600 gigabytes of data, offered it for 60 Bitcoin (about $3.4 million) on the Dark Web, and the breach affected 792,000 people.
segments.texte: 5. In January 2024, hackers from the Rhysida ransomware group attacked Lurie Children’s Hospital in Chicago. Phone numbers, email, electronic medical records and the patient portal went down. Doctors and staff were forced back onto manual procedures. Appointments and surgeries were delayed or cancelled. Why would anyone knowingly hurt children? Money. Rhysida claimed to have stolen around 600 gigabytes of data and put it up for sale on the Dark Web for 60 Bitcoin, worth about $3.4 million. The gang later claimed someone bought it, although that was never independently confirmed. The breach affected a massive 792,000 people. The stolen information potentially included names, addresses, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, diagnoses, treatments, prescriptions and health insurance information.

segments.titre: Why stolen medical data is so valuable
segments.resume: Unlike a credit card, you cannot change your date of birth, Social Security number or medical history, so stolen health records enable identity theft, fraudulent accounts, tax and insurance fraud, convincing phishing and blackmail. This is becoming a huge market on the Dark Web.
segments.texte: In the hacking world, it was a goldmine. If someone steals your credit card details, you call the bank. The card gets cancelled, you change your passwords and another card arrives and life goes on. But you can’t change your date of birth. You can’t easily change your Social Security number. And you can’t change your medical history. Put all that information together and criminals can use it for identity theft, fraudulent accounts, tax and insurance fraud, or highly convincing phishing attacks. And, if the medical information is sensitive, blackmail. This is fast-becoming a huge market on the Dark Web.

segments.titre: Healthcare breach statistics for 2024
segments.resume: In 2024 the US Department of Health and Human Services recorded 663 major healthcare breaches affecting about 243 million individuals, with some people possibly counted more than once. A major study found hacking and IT incidents accounted for 91% of exposed patient records, up from 2% in 2010.
segments.texte: In 2024 alone, the US Department of Health and Human Services recorded 663 major healthcare breaches affecting approximately 243 million individuals. Some people may have been counted more than once, but the scale is still massive. A major study found that hacking and IT incidents accounted for 91% of patient records exposed in healthcare breaches in 2024, up from just 2% in 2010. It’s still happening.

segments.titre: Partnered Health breach in Australia (June 2026)
segments.resume: In June 2026 hackers broke into Australian healthcare provider Partnered Health and stole data from patients at 21 clinics. One expert estimated hackers could earn about $250 per patient's information, which adds up to fortunes at scale.
segments.texte: In June 2026, hackers broke into Australian healthcare provider Partnered Health and stole information from patients at 21 clinics. The data included all kinds of very private information. One expert estimated that hackers could earn around $250 for every patient’s information. Times that by many thousands or millions and someone can get very rich, very fast.

segments.titre: Data brokers and the price of health data: $5 vs $250 to $1,000
segments.resume: The legitimate data-broker industry sells information about ordinary people that criminals combine with hacked data to build detailed victim profiles. Credit card information costs about $5 on the Dark Web while health data sells for $250 to as much as $1,000, around 200 times more, and leaked information stays out forever.
segments.texte: There’s also a huge legitimate data-broker industry collecting and selling information about ordinary people. That information can be combined with data stolen in hacks allowing criminals to build very detailed profiles of their victims. So while you might worry about someone stealing your bank card, it’s your health data that they really want. You can pay $5 for credit card information on the Dark Web and $250 to as much as $1,000 for health data. That’s 200 times more. Once some of that information gets out, it stays out forever. So let’s say you’re not a victim, but a customer. You think you’re safe in the digital shadows. Well, you’re not.

segments.titre: 4. Welcome to Video: the child-abuse site and its customers
segments.resume: About 1.2 million people were members of the Dark Web pornography ring Welcome to Video, including 4,000 paying members in at least 38 countries who downloaded about 360,000 hours of material. The customers believed Tor and Bitcoin payments kept them anonymous.
segments.texte: 4. A very unpleasant fact of life is there are some extremely bad people on this planet we call home. Around 1.2 million of them. That’s how many people were members of a Dark Web pornography ring who used the website Welcome to Video. 4,000 of them were paid members buying content. Spanning at least 38 countries, together they’d downloaded about 360,000 hours of video material. And it was some of the darkest, most depraved material you can imagine. The customers thought they were getting away with it. After all, they’d used a Dark Web website and paid for content with Bitcoin.

segments.titre: How Bitcoin's blockchain exposed Welcome to Video users
segments.resume: Bitcoin's blockchain is a permanent public ledger, and investigators used deanonymization techniques (identity resolution) to match wallet addresses to real identities and trace the site to South Korea. They arrested 337 people across many nationalities, including lecturer Matthew Falder, Hungarian ambassador Gábor Kaleta and former HSI agent Richard Gratkowski.
segments.texte: But even that cannot guarantee anonymity. Bitcoin's blockchain is a permanent public ledger. It’s there for investigators to look at and advances in digital forensics are improving all the time. Investigators use evolving deanonymization techniques in a process known as identity resolution, aka, doxxing. That’s how Welcome to Video customers were brought down. Police matched digital wallet addresses to real-world identities and traced the website back to South Korea. They then arrested a total of 337 people – most of them Koreans but also Americans, British, Germans, Spanish, Saudi Arabian and dozens more nationalities. These people who’d mistakenly believed their secret was safe with the Dark Web were not always obvious criminals. One of the arrested men was Matthew Falder, a Cambridge-educated lecturer. Another was Gábor Kaleta, the Hungarian ambassador to Peru. The haul of depraved Americans included Richard Gratkowski, a former Homeland Security Investigations agent who it turned out had been investigated by his former place of work. Deleting your account doesn't delete the blockchain. A transaction you made years ago can become evidence when investigative technology catches up with you. But let’s also remember that some people go to all the effort to hide themselves while making very amateur mistakes.

segments.titre: 3. Tor onion routing explained
segments.resume: Even people hiding on the Dark Web make ridiculous mistakes. Tor uses onion routing: data is wrapped in three layers and passed through three servers, the entry node knows who you are, the exit node knows where the data goes, and no single server should know both.
segments.texte: 3. You might think these people doing bad things on the Dark Web are sophisticated. After all, they’re already hiding themselves, but sometimes they make the most ridiculous mistakes. The Welcome to Video investigation is proof. The case contains an almost unbelievable blunder made by people who obviously didn’t understand how the Dark Web works. When the authorities were investigating, they looked at the HTML source code of the supposedly hidden Tor website. Tor uses what’s called onion routing – multiple layers of encryption that conceal your online activity. Your data is wrapped in 3 layers and passed through 3 different servers. It’s like giving a message to a friend who passes it to a stranger, who passes it to another stranger. The first, called the entry node, knows who you are but not where you’re going. The middle node passes the data along. The exit node knows where the data is going but not who originally sent it. Each server only peels away its own layer of encryption, so no single server should know both

segments.titre: Welcome to Video admin leaks his server IP in the HTML
segments.resume: The Welcome to Video administrator left the IP address of the real server hosting content inside the website's HTML source code, so police did not need to crack Tor. The IP led to a server in South Korea and to administrator Jong Woo Son, found at his computer with the server running in his bedroom.
segments.texte: who you are and where you’re going. But in the Welcome to Video case, the person running the site managed to undermine all that sophisticated technology with an unbelievably amateur mistake. Hidden inside the website's source code was the IP address of the actual server hosting some of its content. An investigator examining the site's HTML noticed it. Police didn't need to crack Tor. The website itself had told them where to look. Investigators traced the exposed IP address to a server in South Korea and that led them to the front door of the site's administrator, Jong Woo Son. When police raided his home, they reportedly found him sitting at his computer with the server running in his bedroom.

segments.titre: KAX17: hundreds of suspicious Tor relays
segments.resume: Tor requires that the servers a user's data passes through are not controlled by one person, but in 2021 a researcher found the entity KAX17 had been operating hundreds of Tor relays since at least 2017. At its peak over 900 servers, about 14% of guard capacity and 8% of middle-relay capacity, enabled traffic correlation that could kill anonymity.
segments.texte: But here's where things get a little more complex. For this kind of system to work, you have to trust that the different servers your data passes through aren't secretly controlled by the same person. That sounds obvious, but it happened. In 2021, a security researcher discovered that a mysterious entity known as KAX17 had been operating hundreds of Tor relays since at least 2017. Nobody publicly knew who KAX17 was. Nobody knew why he or she or they were doing it. At its peak, the group or person was reportedly operating more than 900 Tor servers. That was about 14% of the network's guard capacity and 8% of its middle-relay capacity. They were essentially guarding the front door and the hallways of the Dark Web. By controlling both ends of the chain, they could instantly match traffic entering Tor with traffic exiting somewhere else. In the cyberworld it’s known as traffic correlation. And it meant anonymity was dead.

segments.titre: Tor's response to KAX17 and theories about who ran it
segments.resume: Journalists and other legitimate users panicked as Tor's developers rushed to remove the suspicious relays, saying there was no evidence any users were unmasked. One theory is that KAX17 was an intelligence agency, since nobody spends years and money taking over an anonymous network for nothing.
segments.texte: It’s an incredible breakthrough if you’re an investigator. But for ordinary users who had perfectly legal reasons to stay hidden - like journalists - KAX17 caused panic for people. Tor's developers rushed to take down the suspicious relays, claiming there was no evidence that any users were unmasked. So, no one got hurt… that we know of. One theory is KAX17 was an intelligence agency. But if it really was harmless, why did a phantom entity spend years - and a considerable amount of money - building it? You don’t take over an anonymous global network just to do nothing. There must have been a very good reason. We can’t talk about the Dark Web and leave out drugs.

segments.titre: 2. Drugs: the biggest Dark Web market
segments.resume: Drugs are by far the biggest Dark Web market, with about $2.6 billion sold in the crypto-enabled illicit economy in 2025. Research found darknet drug buyers reported less exposure to threats and violence than street buyers, and the markets worked like eBay for narcotics with seller ratings and reviews.
segments.texte: 2. Drugs are easily the biggest market on the Dark Web. Nothing else comes close. In 2025, it’s believed $2.6 billion worth was sold in the crypto-enabled illicit economy, a bumper year. And there’s a reason for that. Research found that people buying drugs through darknet markets reported less exposure to threats and violence compared to people buying through traditional markets. Instead of meeting a dealer, you could now access a marketplace through Tor and be presented with a menu of drugs and prices. It was basically eBay for narcotics, complete with seller ratings and customer reviews.

segments.titre: How the Dark Web changed drug dealing: reviews and satisfaction
segments.resume: The 2019 Global Drug Survey found 28.6% of respondents had bought drugs on the Dark Web. Dealers no longer needed street cred, territory or physical intimidation, and buyer reviews created an incentive to sell what was actually advertised.
segments.texte: And it became very popular. The 2019 Global Drug Survey found that 28.6% of respondents had bought drugs from a Dark Web marketplace at some point in their lives. It changed everything. Including the dealers. Traditionally, selling drugs could require street cred, territory and the ability to defend yourself. With the Dark Web, physical intimidation didn’t really matter. Anyone could theoretically become a successful drug dealer without ever having to stand up for himself. But more importantly, it introduced something unexpected to the illegal drug trade: Customer satisfaction. Buyers could review dealers. That created an incentive to sell what you actually advertised.

segments.titre: Risks of buying drugs online vs reliability that saves lives
segments.resume: Buying drugs on the Dark Web is not completely safe, since drugs can be contaminated or counterfeit, markets can steal money, police can watch and packages can be intercepted. Even so, the review system made a bad situation better, and studies show Dark Web drugs can be more reliable than street drugs.
segments.texte: That doesn’t mean buying drugs on the Dark Web is anywhere near completely safe. Drugs can still be contaminated or counterfeit, marketplaces can steal your money, police can be watching and your package can be intercepted. Even so, this review system had for the most part made a bad situation better. Studies have shown that Dark Web drugs can sometimes be more reliable than street drugs and reliability can save lives.

segments.titre: RMIT study: 35% of Dark Web drugs were not as advertised
segments.resume: An RMIT University study tested 103 drugs bought on the Dark Web and found 35% weren't as advertised: 14% had other harmful substances and 21% none of the advertised drug. Only 4 of 19 cocaine samples were pure, while all heroin, MDMA and methamphetamine samples were as promised and ketamine, 2C-B and alprazolam were most likely to be different.
segments.texte: But it’s not perfect. A study led by RMIT University in Australia tested 103 illicit drugs bought through the Dark Web and found 35% weren’t exactly what they were advertised as. Around 14% contained the advertised drug mixed with other psychoactive or potentially harmful substances. 21% contained none of the advertised drugs at all. Cocaine was particularly unreliable. Out of 19 samples, only 4 contained cocaine and nothing else. 13 contained cocaine mixed with other substances and 2 contained no cocaine whatsoever. On the other hand, every sample of heroin, MDMA and methamphetamine tested contained only what the customer had been promised. Drugs sold as ketamine, 2C-B and alprazolam were among the most likely to be something completely different. So, you think you’re guaranteed purity, but that’s not always the case.

segments.titre: European study: 93% matched and cocaine purity of 70%
segments.resume: A larger European study of 129 Dark Web samples found 93% contained the expected drug, and Dark Web cocaine averaged about 70% purity versus 38% for UK street cocaine. Knowing exactly what and how strong a drug is removes one uncertainty, and markets developed their own harm reduction with vendors discussing purity and adulterants.
segments.texte: Well, maybe not. A larger European study tested 129 samples bought from Dark Web markets and found that 93% contained the drug the customer thought they had purchased. And the coke was way stronger on the Dark Web, averaging around 70% purity, compared to 38% for cocaine seized on the streets in the UK at the time. Of course, stronger drugs create dangers of their own. But knowing what substance you’ve actually bought and exactly how strong it is removes at least one of the uncertainties of buying illegal drugs. Many deaths happen because users don’t know what they’re getting. Dark Web markets even developed their own form of harm reduction. Vendors and customers discussed purity, adulterants and safer use, while bad products could receive bad reviews.

segments.titre: Fentanyl and carfentanil sold on Dark Web markets
segments.resume: The darker side of easy drug purchase is that fentanyl and the far more potent carfentanil were available, with researchers identifying dozens of carfentanil vendors. One customer left a 5-star review for a carfentanil supplier while people in Canada were dying from the drug, though buying on the Dark Web might still be safer than the street.
segments.texte: But there is a darker side to making drugs so easy to purchase. You could buy fentanyl. You could even buy the vastly more potent carfentanil. Researchers have identified dozens of vendors advertising carfentanil across Dark Web marketplaces. At a time when people in Canada were dying from the drug, one Dark Web customer left a 5-star review: “Took forever to find a new carfent supplier. Finally found a good vendor!! Great!!!” Even so, if this person was going to buy the drug anyway, maybe Amazon-style drug acquisition was safer than buying on the street. Ok, so you might have heard your cryptocurrency is safe. It’s not.

segments.titre: 1. Bitfinex hack and the 94,000 Bitcoin seizure
segments.resume: In 2022 the Justice Department seized more than 94,000 Bitcoin, worth about $3.6 billion, its largest financial seizure, linked to the 2016 theft of almost 120,000 Bitcoin from exchange Bitfinex. The thief was Ilya Lichtenstein, working with wife Heather Razzlekhan Morgan, who admitted helping launder the money.
segments.texte: 1. In 2022, the Justice Department announced that it had seized more than 94,000 Bitcoin, then worth about $3.6 billion. It was the largest financial seizure in its history. The story goes back to 2016, when someone stole almost 120,000 Bitcoin from the cryptocurrency exchange Bitfinex. At the time, the haul was worth about $70 million but by 2022 that changed considerably. And the thief turned out to be quite a character. His name was Ilya Lichtenstein. He worked alongside his wife, Heather “Razzlekhan” Morgan, a woman who made quite possibly the worst rap music in existence. Morgan would later admit helping launder the stolen money, but it was Lichtenstein who had actually carried out the hack. So how did he steal that much Bitcoin?

segments.titre: How Lichtenstein stole the Bitcoin and why he needed the Dark Web
segments.resume: Bitfinex's multi-key vault included security from BitGo, but Lichtenstein hacked deep enough to fraudulently authorize more than 2,000 withdrawals into a wallet he controlled. Turning billions in stolen Bitcoin into spendable money without getting caught was the hard part, which is where the Dark Web came in.
segments.texte: Bitfinex thought it had built something like a vault requiring more than one key to open. One layer of security was provided by an outside company called BitGo. But Lichtenstein hacked deep enough into Bitfinex’s systems to fraudulently authorize more than 2,000 withdrawals. In the process, thousands of Bitcoin were transferred into a wallet under his control. Stealing it was one thing. Turning billions of dollars of stolen Bitcoin into money you could actually spend without getting caught was something else entirely. This is where the Dark Web enters the story.

segments.titre: Laundering stolen Bitcoin through AlphaBay backfired
segments.resume: Lichtenstein fed some of the stolen Bitcoin through AlphaBay, hoping to obscure the blockchain trail, but the US government seized AlphaBay and its data helped investigators reconstruct the trail. The Dark Web technology he trusted had been made, and is still funded, by the US government.
segments.texte: Lichtenstein started feeding some of the stolen Bitcoin through AlphaBay. The idea was simple: put dirty Bitcoin into a huge anonymous Dark Web marketplace, move it around and withdraw Bitcoin elsewhere. It made the blockchain trail much harder to follow. It might have worked well. Except, as you know, the US government seized AlphaBay because the owner made those amateur mistakes. So, instead of destroying the trail of the missing Bitcoin, AlphaBay helped investigators reconstruct it. The Dark Web technology Lichtenstein had trusted to help hide his billions had been made – and is still being funded – by the US government.

segments.titre: The US government funds Tor: the paradox
segments.resume: Onion routing was developed at the US Naval Research Laboratory, and Tor later became an independent nonprofit that criminals joined. In 2023-24 the Tor Project got about $2.56 million from US government sources, around 35% of its revenue, so one part of the government spends billions hunting criminals while another funds technology that hides them.
segments.texte: Onion routing was developed by researchers at the US Naval Research Laboratory to create anonymous internet communications. Tor later became an independent nonprofit, and inevitably drug dealers, hackers and stolen-data sellers jumped on the anonymity bandwagon. But even with all the reported mayhem of the Dark Web, the US carried on funding Tor. It still does. In 2023–24, the Tor Project received around $2.56 million from US government sources, about 35% of its revenue. So Lichtenstein had effectively used US-funded anonymity technology to help launder his potential billions. And in part, cocaine aficionados demanding greater purity can also thank the US government. But so can dissidents, journalists and even intelligence officers who have very good reasons for wanting to remain anonymous. That’s the paradox. One part of the US government spends billions trying to find criminals hiding on the Dark Web. Meanwhile another spends millions supporting technology designed to make people harder to find.

segments.titre: Why the Dark Web cannot be shut down
segments.resume: Tor is not a single website or company with a server to unplug, and shutting down one marketplace or scammer just leads to others. The network is decentralized with thousands of independent servers, and because the software is open-source, someone else could keep it alive if the Tor Project disappeared.
segments.texte: Even if governments wanted to close down the Dark Web completely, that would be next to impossible. Tor isn't a single website or company with a server someone can just unplug. Shut down one marketplace and another appears. Take down one scammer and others take his place. You can’t stop them. The Tor Project develops the software, but the network is decentralized, with thousands of servers running independently all over the world. And because the software is open-source, even if the Tor Project disappeared tomorrow, someone else could pick up the code and keep it alive.

segments.titre: Scale of stolen data and drug sales in 2024-2025
segments.resume: In 2024 an estimated $1.7 billion in crypto-enabled drug transactions went through the Dark Web, up 20% from the year before. Researchers found 15 billion stolen usernames and passwords, about two per human, and in 2025 credentials from over a million accounts at the world's 100 largest banks were found shared, so your information has probably been in a criminal database.
segments.texte: In 2024, an estimated $1.7 billion in cryptocurrency-enabled drug transactions went through the Dark Web. An increase of 20% from the year before. No one knows how much stolen information exists there because no one can take an inventory of it. But researchers have found 15 billion stolen usernames and passwords circulating through criminal markets, about two for every human being on Earth. In 2025 alone, credentials from more than a million accounts at the world's 100 largest banks were found being shared on Dark Web resources. The Dark Web itself might be small compared with the regular internet but the amount of stolen information circulating through it is anything but. So there’s a good chance that information belonging to many of us has, at some point, ended up in a criminal database.
